## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Sīhacammajātaka* (Ja 189), also rendered as the story of the "Ass in the Lion's Skin," is a canonical verse and narrative found in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Strong 2009]. According to the commentary, the Buddha delivered this tale while residing at Jetavana with reference to the monk Kokālika, who desired to intone or recite chanting (*sarabhañña*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. To illustrate the situation, the Buddha recounts a past life during the reign of King Brahmadatta of Bārāṇasī, in which a merchant dressed his donkey in a lion's skin so that villagers would flee while it grazed in their fields, only for the beast to betray its true identity when it began to bray [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1879]. The central canonical verse opens with the line *N’etaṁ sīhassa naditaṁ* ("Nor lion, nor tiger I see") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879].
Scholars have noted the international circulation of this fable. T. W. Rhys Davids opened his study of the Pali jātakas with a translation of the *Sīhacammajātaka*, highlighting its close parallels in Aesopic fable traditions of Ancient Greece, as well as variants in Medieval Europe, the Near East, China, and wider Indian literature [Strong 2009]. SuttaCentral records four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral]. Automated text-reuse analysis via DharmaNexus identifies no significant Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language alignments for this entry [DharmaNexus].
